A deceased customer's sole heir provides a certified copy of the death certificate and probate grant to a bank, requesting disclosure of the deceased's accounts to administer the estate. A junior bank officer declines.

Is the officer's refusal correct under FSA?

Incorrect — a probate grant makes the heir the legal executor/administrator of the estate. The legal representative can provide written consent for disclosure under Section 134, authorising the bank to release the information.
Correct — the secrecy obligation survives death; no information can be disclosed.
Incorrect — only a court order can compel disclosure for deceased customers.
Correct — the bank must obtain BNM's written approval before disclosing any information to an estate administrator.

FSA Section 134 permits disclosure to the customer's 'legal representative (such as an executor of an estate)' who can provide written permission for disclosure. A probate grant legally appoints the heir as administrator — they can authorise the bank to release information. The officer's refusal is incorrect. A court order would also suffice, but the legal representative's written consent is a separate permitted route.
Under FSA Section 133, the secrecy obligation protects customer information held by financial institutions. Which of the following situations represents a CLEAR BREACH of Section 133?
A bank discloses account information to the police in response to a written request signed by an officer of at least inspector rank.
A bank discloses account information to BNM in response to a written request from BNM.
A bank's compliance manager shares a customer's account details with a competitor bank's CEO during a networking event, claiming it helps them price their services competitively.
A bank discloses account information pursuant to a court order requiring production of records.

Sharing customer account details with a competitor's CEO for pricing purposes is a clear breach of Section 133 — there is no permitted disclosure basis for this. Permitted disclosures under Section 134 include: BNM in writing (B); police request signed by at least an inspector (A); court order (D). Casual disclosure to a competitor for competitive purposes has no legal basis and attracts the RM10 million fine / 5-year imprisonment penalty.
Select the option or combination that CORRECTLY describes the concept of 'Tipping Off' under AMLA and its implications for Reporting Institutions?
Tipping off means providing advance notice of a raid to a money launderer — it is an offence for law enforcement only.
Tipping off only applies to STRs — Threshold Reports can be disclosed to customers.
Tipping off is permitted if the RI believes the information will help identify other suspicious transactions.

Tipping off is prohibited under AMLA — once an STR is filed, the RI must not disclose to the customer or any related person that a report has been made. Violating this prohibition is itself a separate criminal offence.

AMLA prohibits 'tipping off' — once an STR has been filed, the RI and its employees must not inform the subject that a report has been made. This would allow potential money launderers to move funds or destroy evidence. Violating the tipping off prohibition is a separate criminal offence. The prohibition applies to all AMLA reports.

A CFO has two hedging options for a USD10 million receivable due in 90 days:

Option A: Enter a USD/MYR forward contract to sell USD at 4.4500
Option B: Buy USD put options with strike 4.4500, premium RM0.0200 per USD

Under what scenario does Option B (the put option) provide BETTER OUTCOMES than Option A (the forward)?

When USD/MYR at maturity falls BELOW 4.4500 (MYR strengthens more than expected) — both deliver 4.4500; BUT if USD/MYR RISES above 4.4500, the put can be abandoned and USD sold at the higher spot rate, minus the premium cost.
When USD/MYR at maturity is exactly 4.4500 — the option's strike price.
The forward is always better because it has no premium cost.
Option B is never better — options are always inferior to forwards for corporate hedging.

The forward locks in exactly 4.4500. The put option: (1) if USD/MYR falls below 4.4500, exercise the put — locked in at 4.4500 minus the RM0.02 premium; (2) if USD/MYR RISES above 4.4500, abandon the put and sell at the higher spot rate minus the premium. The option provides a floor with upside participation. The put outperforms the forward when MYR weakens beyond the premium cost. Options cost more but provide flexibility.

Under AMLA, Section 14 requires Reporting Institutions to report suspicious transactions. Which of the following is the CORRECT statement about the reporting threshold for STRs?
STRs are only required when transactions exceed RM50,000 in a single transaction.

The trigger is suspicion that the transaction involves proceeds of crime, ML, TF, or PF — regardless of amount. A RM50 test transaction preceding a larger laundering operation should be reported. Under AMLA Section 17, the prescribed retention period for transaction records is 6 years. A bank's system automatically deletes records after 5 years to manage storage costs. The bank is audited and the deletion is discovered.

What is the bank's exposure?
No exposure — 5 years is close enough to 6 years; there is a reasonable tolerance.
Administrative warning only — record retention breaches are not criminal offences.
The bank faces a maximum fine of RM3 million, maximum imprisonment of 5 years for responsible persons, or both — failure to comply with Section 17 retention requirements is a criminal offence.

A bond has a 7% annual coupon (RM70,000 on RM1,000,000 par). An investor is buying the bond 6 months after the last coupon payment. The clean price is RM98.00 per RM100.

What is the DIRTY PRICE (actual consideration) the buyer pays?
RM945,000 — clean price minus accrued interest.
RM1,015,000 — clean price plus accrued interest of RM35,000 (6 months of 7% coupon).
RM1,050,000 — the dirty price always adds a full year's coupon.

Dirty price = RM980,000 + RM35,000 = RM1,015,000. The buyer pays the dirty price — the seller receives compensation for the coupon accrued during their holding period. Clean price is a quotation convention that removes accrued interest variation.

Select the option or combination that scenarios would require a Reporting Institution to apply SIMPLIFIED Customer Due Diligence (as opposed to full CDD or Enhanced Due Diligence)?

Simplified CDD applies to LOWER-RISK customers. A large listed company on Bursa Malaysia Main Market has transparent, publicly available ownership and is subject to continuous regulatory disclosure — this represents lower risk. High-risk jurisdiction customers (A), customers refusing to provide ID (C — RI should decline the relationship), and PEPs (D) all require enhanced, not simplified, CDD. Simplified CDD does not mean no CDD — the RI still verifies identity but with reduced documentation.

An investor buys a put option on a Malaysian equity with a strike price of RM10.00. The option premium paid is RM0.50. At expiry, the stock is trading at RM7.50.

What is the investor's profit or loss at expiry?

A put option gives the right to SELL at the strike price. At expiry with stock at RM7.50: Intrinsic value = RM10.00 - RM7.50 = RM2.50 (in-the-money). Net profit = Intrinsic value - Premium = RM2.50 - RM0.50 = RM2.00 per share. Option A (RM2.50) ignores the premium cost. Option C (loss of RM0.50) would apply if the option expired worthless (stock price above strike).
The market that supports short-term funding and liquidity is the:
The money market supports short-term borrowing, lending and liquidity.

An investor asks: 'Can I sell my structured product to another investor before maturity?' What is the TYPICAL secondary market situation for structured products?

Review the claims below. Which combination is correct?

I. There is generally LIMITED secondary market liquidity for structured products — most are OTC instruments with no exchange listing. An investor wishing to exit before maturity typically has to negotiate directly with the issuing bank (which may or may not provide a bid price), subject to MTM pricing. There is no guaranteed exit.
II. Structured products trade freely on Bursa Malaysia at transparent prices throughout their life.
III. Structured products must be held to maturity by law — secondary sales are prohibited.
IV. Secondary market trading of structured products is highly liquid because banks are required by BNM to maintain two-way markets.

Statement I is true. Secondary market liquidity is a known limitation of structured products. Unlike listed equities or government bonds (which have active secondary markets), most structured products are OTC instruments without exchange listings. Investors wishing to exit before maturity must approach the issuing bank for a bid price — the bank may decline, or offer a price that is substantially below par (reflecting MTM valuation). BNM does not require banks to maintain two-way markets for all structured products. This liquidity risk is explicitly listed as one of the nine structured product risks.

For a complex unlisted capital market product, a short summary document should not merely highlight attractive benefits. It should support informed decision-making by presenting salient information in a clear and concise manner, including key features, key risks, fees, charges, exit-related information and contact points for enquiries or complaints. This document is the:
A Product Highlights Sheet contains clear and concise information on salient product features, key risks, fees, charges and other important information.
A depositor has RM450,000 in each of 1 PIDM member bank. Based on a RM250,000 limit per depositor per member bank, what is the total insured deposit amount?
Coverage is capped at RM250,000 per depositor per member bank. Total insured amount = RM250,000 × 1 = RM250,000.
A bond is best described as:
a debt obligation of an issuing entity
Bonds are debt securities issued to raise funds.

An investor in a 10-year bond at purchase (3% coupon, market yield 5%) has held the bond for 7 years. The remaining maturity is now 3 years and market yields are still 5%. Comparing the price sensitivity (duration) of the bond NOW versus at purchase, which is correct?

From an investor-protection perspective, which statements are true?

I. Duration has DECREASED — with only 3 years remaining (versus 10 at purchase), the bond's duration is now much shorter, meaning its price is much less sensitive to changes in market yields.
II. Duration has increased — more time has passed.
III. Duration is unchanged — it depends only on coupon rate and yield, not on remaining maturity.
IV. Duration has decreased, making the bond a WORSE investment.

Statement I is true. Duration DECREASES as a bond ages (approaches maturity). At purchase: 10-year duration might be ~8 years. After 7 years holding (3 years remaining): duration has shortened significantly to approximately ~2.8 years. This means the bond is now MUCH LESS sensitive to interest rate changes than when first purchased. This 'pull to par' effect also reduces price volatility as maturity approaches. A fund manager wanting to maintain a specific duration target would need to buy new longer-duration bonds as existing holdings age. This is NOT a negative characteristic — it reflects the natural shortening of risk as bonds approach maturity.

Under the MCC, a dealer receives an order from a counterparty to buy USD50 million at 'market.' Before executing, the dealer discusses the order with colleagues in another department who may benefit from trading ahead of the order. Which MCC principle is violated?

Which combination gives the best answer?

I. The transparency principle — the dealer should have disclosed the order to BNM.
II. The confidentiality principle — order information is confidential and must not be shared outside the dealing room.
III. The best execution principle — discussing the order delays execution.
IV. The impartiality principle — the dealer should not favour one department over another.

Statement II is true. Under the MCC, dealers have an obligation of CONFIDENTIALITY regarding order information. A client's pending order (particularly a large USD50 million order) is market-sensitive — sharing it with colleagues in another department who might trade ahead of it (front-running) is a serious confidentiality breach. The confidentiality principle protects clients from having their orders used by others to profit at the client's expense. This is also connected to the client order priority principle (Section 93 CMSA) — but the specific MCC principle breached is confidentiality.

Under CMSA, the SC issues a written demand for a company's internal documents during a market misconduct investigation. The company's lawyer says some documents may be protected by legal professional privilege, but this must be assessed document by document.

Which statements should remain in the client explanation?

I. Legal professional privilege always overrides all regulatory document demands.
II. Legal professional privilege does not exist in Malaysia, so all documents must be produced.
III. Legal professional privilege may protect certain legal-advice documents, but the SC has broad investigative powers and the company must obtain specific legal advice on what is protected.
IV. The SC's CMSA powers override all forms of privilege without exception.

Statement III is true. Legal professional privilege may protect certain confidential lawyer-client communications, but it is not a blanket answer to every regulatory document demand. The company should assess the documents specifically and obtain legal advice because the SC has broad investigative powers under CMSA.
A primary market is mainly used for:
Primary markets are used for new securities issuance.

Malaysia's Employees Provident Fund (EPF) invests heavily in Malaysian Government Securities (MGS). When MGS yields fall, what happens to the value of EPF's existing MGS portfolio and why?

Assess the statements below and select the correct combination.

I. MGS values RISE when yields fall — bond prices move inversely to yields. When market yields fall below the coupon rate of existing bonds, those bonds become more valuable because their fixed coupons are now above the market rate, attracting buyers who push prices up.
II. MGS values fall when yields fall — lower yields mean less income.
III. MGS values are unaffected by yield changes since they are government-guaranteed at par.
IV. MGS values rise slightly but the effect is negligible for large portfolios.

Statement I is true. The inverse price-yield relationship applies to all bonds including MGS. When market yields fall: (1) existing MGS paying higher coupons become more attractive; (2) buyers compete to acquire these higher-coupon bonds; (3) prices are bid up until the yield on the bond equals the new market yield. EPF's existing MGS portfolio therefore INCREASES in market value when yields fall — generating unrealised capital gains. Government guarantee is about credit risk (repayment at maturity), not about price volatility — prices still fluctuate with market yields.

A market participant is concerned about CMSA's whistleblowing provisions. Which of the following CORRECTLY describes how CMSA protects persons who report suspected breaches?

Which set of statements should the RM accept as accurate?

I. CMSA has no specific whistleblower protections — reporters rely on general contract law.
II. Persons who report in good faith to the SC about suspected CMSA contraventions are afforded protection — their identity is kept confidential and they are protected from civil and criminal liability for the disclosure.
III. Whistleblowers must first obtain a court order before reporting to the SC.
IV. Only employees of licensed institutions can report under CMSA's whistleblowing provisions.

Statement II is true. CMSA and the Whistleblower Protection Act 2010 protect persons who report suspected contraventions to the SC in good faith. Protections include: confidentiality of the reporter's identity; immunity from civil and criminal liability for making the report (as long as the report was made in good faith). This encourages reporting of market misconduct without fear of retaliation. Whistleblowing is open to any person — not limited to licensed institution employees. No prior court order is required.

Malaysia is a member of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). What are the primary AML obligations that FATF membership imposes on Malaysian Reporting Institutions?

Review the claims below. Which combination is correct?

I. FATF membership requires Malaysian banks to physically inspect all cash deposited.
II. FATF membership only applies to international transactions — domestic transactions are exempt.
III. FATF standards (which Malaysia has adopted through BNM guidelines) require RIs to: implement CDD, maintain records, file STRs, implement compliance programmes, and apply targeted financial sanctions — the 'FATF 40 Recommendations' form the basis of Malaysia's AML/CFT framework.
IV. FATF requires all Malaysian banks to share customer data with foreign regulators automatically.

Statement III is true. Malaysia as a FATF member implements the FATF 40 Recommendations through its domestic legislation (AMLA) and BNM guidelines. These require RIs to: (1) conduct Customer Due Diligence (CDD) and Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD); (2) maintain transaction records for 6 years; (3) file Suspicious Transaction Reports; (4) implement compliance programmes including training and independent audit; (5) apply Targeted Financial Sanctions (TFS) for proliferation financing. FATF standards apply to all transactions (not just international), and automatic data sharing with foreign regulators requires specific legal frameworks (MoUs, etc.).
In an 80-question mock exam, a candidate answers 60 questions correctly. What percentage score did the candidate achieve?
Score percentage = correct answers / total questions × 100 = 60 / 80 × 100 = 75%.

A stockbroking firm holds a Capital Markets Services Licence (CMSL) for dealing in securities. One of its senior analysts regularly writes research reports recommending stocks and bonds to institutional clients. Which module or licence authorisation covers the analyst's activity?

I. The analyst needs a separate CMSL authorisation specifically for 'investment advice' as a distinct regulated activity under CMSA.
II. The analyst needs a separate BNM licence for investment advice.
III. The analyst's research distribution is covered under the firm's CMSL for dealing in securities — research and investment advice for clients of a licensed dealer is encompassed within the CMSL framework.
IV. The analyst is unregulated — only dealers executing trades need CMSL authorisation.

Statement I is true. Under CMSA, 'investment advice' is a separate regulated activity listed in Schedule 2 of CMSA. While a stockbroking firm's CMSL for dealing covers execution, the PROVISION OF INVESTMENT ADVICE as a standalone activity to clients requires specific authorisation under the CMSL. The firm's existing dealing licence does not automatically cover investment advice if that advice is provided as a standalone service. The analyst's reports constituting 'investment advice' require the firm to hold the appropriate CMSL authorisation.

An investor is short a call option on a Malaysian equity (they SOLD a call option to another party). The stock price rises significantly above the strike price. What is the financial position of the short call option holder?

I. The short call holder profits from the price rise.
II. The short call holder faces UNLIMITED potential losses — they must sell the stock to the option buyer at the strike price regardless of how high the market price goes. If they do not own the stock (naked short), the loss can theoretically be unlimited.
III. The short call holder's maximum loss is limited to the option premium received.
IV. The short call holder can simply refuse to honour the option if the price moves too far.

Statement II is true. A short call writer has UNLIMITED potential loss: the option buyer will exercise the call if the stock rises above the strike price, and the call writer must deliver shares at the (lower) strike price. If the writer sold a 'naked' call (without owning the underlying shares), they must buy shares in the market at whatever price they have risen to — theoretically unlimited. The premium received (option B) is the MAXIMUM PROFIT, not the maximum loss. The maximum LOSS is unlimited (for naked calls) or the profit foregone (for covered calls). The writer cannot refuse to honour a validly exercised option.

A licensed securities dealer's CMSL covers 'dealing in securities.' One of its dealers advises a sophisticated investor client on which bonds to buy without executing the actual trade (the client uses another broker to execute). Does the dealer need additional authorisation to provide this standalone investment advice?

From an investor-protection perspective, which statements are true?

I. No — a CMSL for dealing in securities covers all investment advice activities.
II. No — investment advice to sophisticated investors is always unregulated.
III. Yes — 'investment advice' is a SEPARATE regulated activity under CMSA. Providing standalone investment advice (not incidental to executing a trade) requires a separate authorisation on the CMSL.
IV. Yes — but only if the advice concerns Islamic securities.

Statement III is true. Under CMSA Schedule 2, the regulated activities include both 'dealing in securities' and 'investment advice' as SEPARATE activities. A CMSL for 'dealing in securities' covers execution and dealing but does not automatically cover providing standalone investment advice. If a licensed dealer provides investment advice as a distinct service (not merely incidental to executing a trade), a separate 'investment advice' authorisation is required. Sophisticated investor status does not eliminate the regulatory authorisation requirement.

Review the statements below.

I. PIDM administers deposit insurance.
II. PIDM helps support confidence.

What should the RM conclude?

Under CMSA, a 'Capital Markets Services Representative's Licence' (CMSRL) is required for individuals. Which of the following is CORRECT about the CMSRL?
An individual can perform regulated activities under their employer's CMSL without a personal CMSRL.

An individual who performs regulated capital market activities on behalf of a CMSL holder must hold a personal CMSRL — the CMSL is the firm's licence; the CMSRL is the individual's licence. Both must be in place.
The CMSRL was abolished by CMSA — only corporate CMSL licences are required.
The CMSRL applies only to dealing in equities — bond dealing requires a different licence.

CMSA establishes a dual licensing structure: the CMSL (Capital Markets Services Licence) is the corporate/firm-level licence held by the institution. The CMSRL (Capital Markets Services Representative's Licence) is the individual-level licence held by the specific person performing regulated activities on behalf of the CMSL holder. Both must be in force. An individual cannot perform regulated activities (dealing, advising, fund management) on behalf of a licensed firm without holding their own CMSRL. This creates individual accountability alongside corporate accountability.

Review the statements below in relation to anti-money laundering controls and customer due diligence expectations.

I. Customer due diligence is required when establishing a business relationship.
II. Enhanced due diligence may be relevant where risk factors indicate higher risk.
III. Incomplete beneficial ownership information can be ignored whenever a relationship appears commercially valuable.
IV. Layering is the final stage where illicit funds are enjoyed after they have already been fully absorbed into the economy.
I and II only — both statements reflect core due diligence and risk-based control expectations
I and III only — commercial value can replace verification where the relationship is important
II and IV only — layering is the final enjoyment stage after funds are absorbed
III and IV only — both statements support simplified treatment for higher-value relationships
Statements I and II are correct. Commercial value does not remove due diligence duties, and layering disguises the trail of funds.
AMLA distinguishes between 'terrorism financing' and 'money laundering.' Which of the following CORRECTLY identifies a key difference between the two?
Terrorism financing always involves larger amounts than money laundering.

Money laundering involves concealing the PROCEEDS of crime (dirty money being cleaned). Terrorism financing may involve LEGITIMATE funds being channelled toward terrorist activities — the funds may be clean but the PURPOSE is criminal. Both require RIs to monitor and report suspicious activities.
Terrorism financing is regulated by the police; money laundering is regulated by BNM.
Both terms describe identical activities — there is no meaningful distinction.

This is a critical distinction: Money laundering = transforming dirty (criminal proceeds) money into apparently clean money. Terrorism financing = funding terrorist activities — the SOURCE of funds may be legitimate (charitable donations, business income, personal savings) but the INTENDED USE is for terrorism. This is why AML/CFT programs address both — pure ML monitoring might not detect legitimate funds being diverted to terrorism. RIs must monitor for both, including understanding the SOURCE and PURPOSE of funds, not just their origin.

Review the statements below.

I. Bonds are debt obligations.
II. Sukuk are Islamic securities.
III. Bonds always remove default risk.
IV. Debt securities are ordinary shares.
Statements I and II are correct.

An investor holds a bond with a 10% coupon when market rates were 10% (purchased at par). Over the next 3 years, rates fall to 7%, then recover to 9%, then rise to 11%.

At the end of 3 years, the investor's realised return compared to the original YTM of 10% will be:
Exactly 10% — YTM at purchase is always the realised return.
Less than 10% — rates ultimately ended higher than the purchase YTM, meaning the bond is now trading at a discount and the investor has a capital loss relative to par.
More than 10% — rates fell below 10% during the period, generating capital gains.
Cannot be determined without knowing whether the investor sold during the rate moves.

The realised return depends on whether the investor holds to maturity or sells, and at what prices coupons were reinvested. YTM at purchase (10%) is the PROMISED return only if the investor holds to maturity AND reinvests all coupons at exactly 10%. Over 3 years with volatile rates: (1) coupons may have been reinvested at different rates; (2) if the investor still holds the bond, it is now trading below par (rates at 11% > coupon 10%); (3) interim price changes affect mark-to-market but not realised return if held to maturity. The answer: WITHOUT knowing the actual reinvestment rates AND whether the bond is sold, the realised return truly cannot be determined from rate history alone.
Using the approximate Fisher relationship, a nominal interest rate is 8% and inflation is 3%. What is the approximate real interest rate?
Approximate real interest rate = nominal rate − inflation rate = 8% − 3% = 5%.

A bank officer is approached by a journalist writing about a high-profile fraud case involving one of the bank's customers. The journalist says: 'The information I need is already in the public domain — it appeared in a court judgment. So you can confirm the details.' 

Is the journalist's reasoning correct?
Yes — once information is in the public domain through a court judgment, the bank can freely discuss it.

No — even if information appeared in a published court judgment, this does not create a permitted disclosure basis under FSA Section 133 for the bank to independently confirm or provide additional customer information to a journalist. The bank must still comply with Section 133.
Yes — court judgments are public documents and FSA Section 133 does not apply to publicly available information.
Yes — journalists have a statutory right to access financial information for reporting purposes.

The appearance of information in a court judgment does not create a general permission for the bank to confirm or elaborate on customer information to journalists. Section 133 of FSA requires the bank to maintain secrecy of customer information unless a specific Section 134 exception applies. A journalist request is not listed as a permitted disclosure. The bank should refer the journalist to the published court record itself and decline to provide independent confirmation of customer information.
The regulator responsible for Malaysia’s capital market is:
The SC regulates Malaysia’s capital market.

What should the product or compliance team do?

The Malaysian bond market includes both Ringgit-denominated and foreign currency-denominated bonds. Which of the following CORRECTLY describes who can issue bonds denominated in currencies other than Ringgit in the Malaysian market?
Only Malaysian government entities may issue foreign currency bonds in Malaysia.
Only foreign corporations and multilateral institutions (such as the World Bank) may issue foreign currency bonds in Malaysia — these are called 'Samurai bonds' or 'Dragon bonds.'

Both Malaysian and foreign issuers may issue foreign currency bonds in Malaysia with the relevant approvals; these include Ringgit bonds issued by multilateral development banks (known as 'Samurai bonds' in Japan but called 'Barakah bonds' or similar locally).
Foreign entities may issue Ringgit-denominated bonds in Malaysia (known as 'foreign currency bonds' locally) but must hedge the currency risk through BNM.

Foreign entities (including multilateral development banks, foreign governments, and foreign corporations) may issue Ringgit-denominated bonds in Malaysia — these are sometimes called 'foreign issuer Ringgit bonds.' Foreign currency bond issuances in Malaysia also occur with proper approvals. The key point: both Malaysian and foreign issuers participate in Malaysia's bond market, in both Ringgit and foreign currency denominations. 'Samurai bonds' refers to Yen bonds issued in Japan by non-Japanese entities — a different market.

Which answer reflects the correct investor-protection outcome?

The Financial Services Act 2013 (FSA) replaced an earlier Act. Which Act did FSA replace, and what was the KEY change in supervisory scope?

FSA replaced the Banking and Financial Institutions Act 1989 (BAFIA); key change was consolidating regulation of conventional banks, insurance companies, and payment system operators under a single Act.
FSA replaced the Securities Commission Act 1993; key change was creating the self-funding mechanism for BNM.
FSA replaced the Securities Industry Act 1983; key change was moving bond market regulation from BNM to the SC.
FSA replaced the Companies Act 1965; key change was regulating corporate governance.

FSA 2013 replaced BAFIA 1989. The key change was consolidating in a single Act the regulation of: conventional commercial banks, investment banks, insurance companies, and payment system operators. This rationalised the regulatory framework under BNM. BAFIA governed conventional banking but had a narrower scope. The Securities Industry Act 1983 was replaced by CMSA 2007, not FSA. The SC regulates the capital market; BNM's self-funding status predates FSA.

The MCC requires dealers to document the basis for all deals. A dealer closes a large FX transaction on the phone without any written confirmation until the following day when the rate has moved significantly against the counterparty. The counterparty disputes the deal.

What does the MCC require in this situation?
The counterparty's verbal confirmation during the call is sufficient — no documentation needed if both parties verbally agreed.

All deals must be confirmed in writing promptly — the MCC requires deal confirmations to be issued immediately or as soon as possible after execution. Late confirmation (the next day) after the rate has moved is a compliance failure and may suggest an attempt to take advantage of price movements.
Documentation is only required for deals exceeding RM10 million.
Documentation can be deferred for up to 5 business days for complex transactions.

The MCC requires timely documentation of all deals — confirmations should be issued promptly after execution, not deferred until the following day. Same-day confirmation (or immediate electronic confirmation) is the standard. Deferring confirmation until the next day (after rates have moved) creates the appearance that the dealer is selectively confirming only deals that moved in their favour, and cherry-picking prices to the counterparty's detriment. This raises serious conduct and integrity concerns under the MCC.
A principal-protected structured investment commonly combines a protection component with:
Principal-protected structures commonly combine protection and derivative components.

A structured product is marketed as 'guaranteed.' The marketing materials show a graph of historical simulated returns. A customer asks: 'Is the guarantee from the Malaysian government?'

What is the correct answer?
Yes — all guaranteed structured products carry implicit government backing.
Yes — PIDM guarantees all structured products up to RM250,000.

No — the 'guarantee' in a structured product typically refers to the issuer's (usually a bank's) promise to return the principal at maturity, subject to the issuer's own credit risk. It is NOT a government guarantee. The customer's ability to receive the guaranteed amount depends on the bank remaining solvent.
The guarantee is backed by both the government and PIDM jointly.

'Guaranteed' in a structured product context means the issuing bank promises to return the principal at maturity — it is the BANK'S guarantee, not the government's. This guarantee is subject to the bank's credit risk — if the bank becomes insolvent, the guarantee may not be honoured (structured products are typically NOT PIDM-eligible since they are usually based on NIDs which are explicitly excluded). Customers must understand they are exposed to the issuing bank's credit risk. The word 'guaranteed' in marketing can be misleading if customers assume government backing.

A bond fund manager uses 'immunisation' to protect a RM100 million pension fund against interest rate risk, targeting a specific liability due in 6 years. The manager sets the portfolio duration to exactly 6 years.

After 1 year, the portfolio duration has naturally shortened. What must the manager do to maintain immunisation?
Nothing — once immunised, a portfolio remains immunised forever without adjustment.

The manager must REBALANCE the portfolio — as time passes, the portfolio's duration naturally shortens (bonds age). To maintain the 6-year target duration match with the now-5-year-remaining liability, the manager must sell shorter-duration bonds and buy longer-duration bonds to extend the portfolio's duration back to 5 years.
The manager must sell ALL bonds and reinvest in new 6-year bonds annually.
The manager must increase the portfolio's cash holding to reduce duration.

Immunisation requires ongoing rebalancing. After 1 year: the liability due in 6 years is now 5 years away → target duration is now 5 years. The portfolio's duration has also naturally shortened (bonds have aged by 1 year) — but not by exactly the same amount. To maintain the duration match: the manager must sell bonds whose duration has dropped below the new target and buy bonds with duration that restores the portfolio to a 5-year duration. This rebalancing is required periodically (typically quarterly or when interest rates change materially). Immunisation is NOT a set-and-forget strategy.

What should be done or concluded based on the scenario?

A bond investor reads in the trust deed: 'The issuer must maintain a Debt-to-Equity ratio of no more than 2.0x at all times; violation of this covenant is an Event of Default.'

What type of covenant is this and what protection does it provide?
A positive (affirmative) covenant — it requires the issuer to do something.

A negative (restrictive) covenant — it RESTRICTS the issuer from exceeding a financial ratio, protecting bondholders by limiting the issuer's ability to take on excessive leverage beyond 2.0x D/E, which could impair its ability to service the bonds.
A call provision — it gives the issuer the right to repay early.
An acceleration clause — it allows the trustee to demand immediate repayment.

A NEGATIVE covenant (also called a restrictive covenant) RESTRICTS the issuer from doing certain things. In this case: restricts the issuer from allowing its debt-to-equity ratio to exceed 2.0x. This protects bondholders by limiting the amount of additional leverage the issuer can take on — excessive leverage increases default risk. If violated, it triggers an Event of Default, allowing bondholders (through the trustee) to take protective action. A POSITIVE covenant requires the issuer TO DO something (e.g., maintain insurance, provide audited accounts). An acceleration clause would be the consequence of the default, not the covenant itself.
A bond is priced at RM100 and has modified duration of 3. If yield rises by 1.00 percentage points, what is the approximate new price using duration approximation?
Approximate % price change = −modified duration × change in yield. = −3 × 1.00% = -3.00%. New price ≈ RM100 × (1 -0.0300) = RM97.

A Malaysian bank has been fined by US regulators for AML deficiencies in its New York branch. The bank's management says: 'The New York branch is separately incorporated — Malaysian AML regulations don't apply there.'

Is this reasoning correct under AMLA Section 19?
Yes — overseas branches and subsidiaries are entirely separate legal entities and Malaysian AML does not apply to them.

No — Section 19 of AMLA requires compliance programmes to be implemented on branches and subsidiaries INTERNATIONALLY. The bank's Malaysian-standard AML/CFT framework must be applied globally, including to the New York branch.
Yes — only Malaysian-based transactions are subject to AMLA requirements.
Partially — Section 19 applies to overseas subsidiaries but not to overseas branches of the same legal entity.

Section 19 of AMLA explicitly requires RIs to implement compliance programmes on 'branches and subsidiaries internationally.' This means the Malaysian bank's AML/CFT standards apply globally — including to the New York branch. If the New York branch is deficient, this is also a Malaysian regulatory concern in addition to the US regulatory action. The reasoning that overseas branches are separate is incorrect from a Malaysian AML perspective. Where local (US) requirements are MORE stringent, the stricter standard applies.

A product recommendation made purely because of sales targets, without practical steps to understand objectives, financial situation and particular needs, creates a capital market conduct concern. The central weakness is that the recommendation lacks proper investigation and relevant profile information. This is best described as absence of:
Section 92 requires a reasonable basis for recommendations.

Which option avoids the common exam trap?

Under BNM's FEA Rules, which of the following CORRECTLY describes when a Malaysian resident requires BNM's prior approval to make an investment in a foreign country?
Any investment in a foreign country always requires BNM prior approval.

Malaysian residents investing in foreign currency assets generally do not require BNM prior approval if they have no Ringgit borrowings. However, INVESTMENTS IN FOREIGN COUNTRIES exceeding USD50 million per calendar year by resident companies may require prior BNM approval or notification.
Foreign investment is prohibited for all Malaysian residents under FEA Rules.
Prior approval is required only for investments in countries without free trade agreements with Malaysia.

The FEA Rules have been significantly liberalised. Generally, Malaysian residents without Ringgit borrowings are free to invest in foreign currency assets without BNM prior approval. For resident companies, there is a USD50 million threshold per calendar year — investments above this amount may require BNM notification or approval. The rules are not a blanket prohibition on foreign investment, and they are not tied to free trade agreements. The key variable is whether the investor has domestic Ringgit borrowings (which restricts FCY investing) and the investment amount.
Required due diligence information is not provided. What should be considered?
Do not proceed and consider suspicious reporting
Ignore the issue for large amounts
Where CDD cannot be completed, the relationship should not proceed and reporting may be considered.

What should the product or compliance team do?

The Malaysian Secondary Mortgage Corporation, Cagamas Berhad, issues both conventional and Islamic debt. Its Islamic bonds are called 'Sanadat Mudharabah Cagamas.'

Which concept underpins Sanadat Mudharabah Cagamas?
Ijarah — the bonds represent a lease of mortgage assets to investors.
Musyarakah — investors and Cagamas jointly own a pool of mortgages.
Mudharabah — Cagamas acts as the Mudarib (manager) of a pool of Islamic home financing assets, with investors as the Rabbul Mal (capital providers) sharing in the profits generated by those assets.
Murabahah — Cagamas sells mortgages to investors at a cost-plus-profit margin.

Sanadat Mudharabah Cagamas are based on the MUDHARABAH concept: Cagamas is the Mudarib (fund manager/entrepreneur) managing a pool of Islamic home financing assets. Investors are the Rabbul Mal (capital providers) who provide funds. Profits generated by the underlying Islamic financing assets are shared between Cagamas (as Mudarib) and investors (as Rabbul Mal) according to the agreed profit-sharing ratio. In losses (not due to negligence), the capital providers bear the loss while Cagamas loses only its effort. The 'Mudharabah' in the name is the key Shariah concept employed.

Which response best resolves this case?

A structured product investor wants to compare the 'total cost of investment.' Which of the following costs might be EMBEDDED in a structured product but are NOT separately itemised in the product's marketing materials?

The ZNID margin (the difference between the ZNID's actual internal return and what the investor implicitly earns on the protected portion), the option pricing spread, and the issuer's profit margin — all embedded in the product's structure rather than listed as explicit fees.
The product's tenor — this is always prominently disclosed.
The credit rating of the issuer — this is regulated information that must be disclosed.
The minimum investment amount — this is always disclosed in the term sheet.

Structured products have costs embedded in their structure that are not visible as explicit fees: (1) The spread on the ZNID (the issuing bank may purchase the ZNID at a lower rate than what could be obtained in the market); (2) the option pricing spread (the bank prices the option at more than it costs in the market, keeping the spread); (3) the issuer's overall structuring margin. These are separate from any explicit fees listed. Investors see the participation rate and principal protection level — but the embedded costs reduce the effective participation rate below what could theoretically be achieved at arm's length. This is why 'price discovery' in structured products is challenging for individual investors.
Under BNM's AML/CFT guidelines, Reporting Institutions must conduct Customer Due Diligence on beneficial owners. What is a 'beneficial owner' in the context of a corporate customer?
The beneficial owner is the company's external auditor who reviews the accounts.
The beneficial owner is the bank relationship manager who manages the account.
The beneficial owner is the director who signs the account opening documents.

A bond's modified duration is 5.5 years. Its convexity is 65. Market yields fall by 100 basis points (1%).

Using the duration-convexity approximation, what is the approximate percentage price INCREASE?

Price change ≈ (-Duration × Δy) + (½ × Convexity × Δy²). For a yield DECREASE of 1% (Δy = -0.01): = (-5.5 × (-0.01)) + (0.5 × 65 × 0.0001) = 0.055 + 0.00325 = 0.05825 = 5.825% ≈ 5.8%. The duration component gives +5.5% (yield fell, price rises). The convexity adjustment is always POSITIVE (enhances the price rise when yields fall, and reduces the price fall when yields rise). Without convexity: 5.5% increase; with convexity: 5.8% increase. Convexity is an asymmetric advantage for bondholders.

An investor calculates the 'Yield to Worst' (YTW) on a callable bond. What does Yield to Worst represent?
The yield assuming the bond defaults immediately.
The yield at which the bond has the maximum duration, representing the highest interest rate risk.
The yield earned if the investor sells the bond at the worst possible price.

The LOWEST possible yield an investor can achieve on the bond, calculated as the minimum of the Yield to Call (at each possible call date) and the Yield to Maturity — representing the worst-case yield scenario for the investor if the issuer acts in the most unfavourable manner.

Yield to Worst (YTW) is calculated as the MINIMUM of: YTM (if held to final maturity) and YTC (calculated at each possible call date). For a callable bond, the issuer will call when it is in the issuer's interest (when rates fall). YTW tells the investor the worst possible yield they will earn, regardless of when the issuer calls. Investors use YTW to evaluate callable bonds conservatively — assuming the issuer will act in its own best interest (calling the bond at the most disadvantageous time for the investor).

The Malaysian bond market uses 'coupon stripping' for certain government bonds. What is coupon stripping and what instruments does it create?

Coupon stripping involves separating the coupon payments from the principal of a conventional coupon bond — each coupon and the final principal repayment become separate zero coupon instruments (called 'strips'), each traded at a discount to its face value.
Coupon stripping reduces the coupon rate by refinancing — it is a cost-reduction technique for bond issuers.
Coupon stripping is the process of converting an Islamic bond to a conventional bond.
Coupon stripping removes all coupon payments from a bond, converting it to a perpetual instrument.

Coupon stripping ('bond stripping') separates a conventional coupon bond into its component cash flows. For a 5-year bond paying 6 semi-annual coupons + principal: stripping creates 10 semi-annual coupon strips (each a small zero coupon bond due on the coupon date) + 1 principal strip (a large zero coupon bond due at maturity). Each strip trades separately at a discount to its face value. Strips allow investors to create customised cash flow profiles without reinvestment risk, since each strip matures at a known date for a known amount.

In a structured product, the issuer combines two elements: (1) a Zero Coupon NID that pays RM1,000,000 at maturity; and (2) a call option on the KLCI. The investor pays RM900,000 upfront.

Which of the following CORRECTLY identifies how the RM900,000 is allocated between the two components?
RM900,000 entirely to buy the call option; ZNID is provided free.
RM900,000 is split exactly 50:50 between the ZNID and the call option.

Most of the RM900,000 goes to purchase the ZNID at a discount (e.g., RM860,000) — which grows to RM1,000,000 at maturity providing the capital protection; the remainder (RM40,000) is used to purchase the call option providing the equity upside.
The RM900,000 goes entirely to the ZNID; the call option is purchased using the issuer's profits.

The classic principal-protected structured product split: The PV of the ZNID equals approximately RM860,000 (growing to RM1,000,000 at maturity — this is the capital protection component). Remaining = RM900,000 - RM860,000 = RM40,000 (less any issuer fees) → used to buy the call option (the equity upside component). The ZNID is purchased at a deep discount; the difference between the purchase price and par represents the return of principal guarantee. The option budget is whatever is left after funding the ZNID and covering fees. This split is the foundation of ALL principal-protected structured product design.

A bond has a face value of RM1,000,000 and matures in exactly 2 years. It pays NO coupon. The market yield is 5.5%.

RM898,452 — use Yield to Maturity (YTM) as the appropriate measure; zero coupon bonds have no coupons to reinvest so YTM = realised return if held to maturity.
RM900,367 — use current yield as it reflects income.
RM1,000,000 — zero coupon bonds are always priced at par.

Zero coupon bond price = Par ÷ (1 + r)^n = 1,000,000 ÷ (1.055)^2 = 1,000,000 ÷ 1.113025 = RM898,452. YTM is the appropriate measure because zero coupon bonds have no coupons — current yield = 0 (meaningless). YTM captures the total return from buying at a discount and receiving par at maturity. Zero coupon bonds eliminate reinvestment risk — the YTM is guaranteed if held to maturity since there are no intermediate cash flows to reinvest at potentially different rates. Price must be below par since there are no coupons.

A bond has a par value of RM1,000,000, a 5% annual coupon, and 6 years to maturity. The market yield is 7%. Calculate the price using the PV formula.

Which of the following is CLOSEST to the correct price?

PV of coupons + PV of par. Annual coupon = RM50,000. At 7% for 6 years: PV annuity factor = [1-(1.07)^-6]/0.07 = [1-0.6663]/0.07 = 0.3337/0.07 = 4.767. PV coupons = 50,000 × 4.767 = RM238,350. PV par = 1,000,000/(1.07)^6 = 1,000,000/1.5007 = RM666,342. Total price = 238,350 + 666,342 = RM904,692 ≈ RM904,767. Since yield (7%) > coupon (5%), bond trades at a DISCOUNT — options B and C (at or above par) are immediately eliminated. Option D (RM857,142) would imply an even higher yield.

This pattern is 'structuring' — deliberately keeping transactions below the reporting threshold to avoid triggering Cash Threshold Reports. It is a well-known money laundering technique. Under AMLA, structuring is itself suspicious activity — the obligation to file an STR is based on SUSPICION, not on individual transaction amounts. A long-standing customer relationship does not reduce the obligation to investigate and report suspicious patterns. The bank must not tip off the customer, but must investigate and file an STR if suspicion is established.

Under the MCC, a dealer receives a 'stop-loss' order from a client: 'Sell my USD10 million position if USD/MYR falls below 4.40.' The rate drops to 4.3950 briefly during a thin market, triggering the stop-loss. The dealer executes at 4.3900 (the first available price after the trigger).

Is the dealer's execution compliant with the MCC?

Compliant — a stop-loss order becomes a market order when triggered. Execution at 4.3900 (the first available price after the 4.4000 trigger was breached) is appropriate given market conditions. The dealer executed as soon as practicable at the best available price.
Non-compliant — the stop-loss should have been executed exactly at 4.4000 (the trigger price).
Non-compliant — stop-loss orders may only be executed during normal market hours and cannot trigger in thin markets.
Non-compliant — the dealer should have warned the client before executing in a thin market.

A stop-loss order becomes a MARKET ORDER when the trigger level is reached — the dealer must then execute at the best available price in the market. In a thin market, the best available price after the 4.4000 trigger may be 4.3900 or even lower. The client's instruction was to SELL IF the rate fell below 4.4000 — not to sell at exactly 4.4000. Execution at 4.3900 (the first available fill) is the correct and compliant response. Waiting for a better price would violate the spirit of the stop-loss instruction.
